title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(d)(1) Qualified Research Defined
description: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), qualified research must meet a four-part test, from Section 174A eligibility to a process of experimentation.
summary: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), qualified research for the federal R&D tax credit must meet a cumulative four-part test: Section 174A expenditure eligibility, discovery of technological information, a new or improved business component, and a process of experimentation covering at least 80 percent of activities. Taxpayers claiming federal or state credits, including California's, must substantiate each test.

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), qualified research for the federal R&D tax credit must meet a cumulative four-part test: Section 174A expenditure eligibility, discovery of technological information, a new or improved business component, and a process of experimentation covering at least 80 percent of activities. Taxpayers claiming federal or state credits, including California's, must substantiate each test.

Under 26 U.S.C. Section 41(d)(1), the federal income tax framework restricts the definition of "qualified research" to research (A) with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A, (B) that is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature and the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and (C) substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in Section 41(d)(3). The cross-reference in subparagraph (A) was rewritten by Public Law 119-21, title VII, § 70302(b)(2)(A), enacted July 4, 2025 (commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or OBBBA). For taxable years beginning in 2022 through 2024, the same subparagraph referred to "specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174," and before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act it referred to expenses that could be treated as "expenses under section 174." The substance of the test has not changed across these versions: this four-part statutory architecture operates as a cumulative legal filter that separates systematic scientific and engineering work from routine product development, quality control, cosmetic design, and unguided adjustments made until something works.

The definitional boundaries established in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) serve not only as the threshold for the federal credit for increasing research activities under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a), but also as the foundational eligibility standard for state-level research tax incentives that incorporate Section 41 by reference. The most prominent of these is the California Research and Development Tax Credit under California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) Section 23609, and this report also compares the New York and Massachusetts regimes. Evaluating 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) requires examining the statutory text, the Treasury Regulations under 26 CFR § 1.41-4, the legislative history of the Tax Reform Act of 1986, federal and state judicial and administrative precedents, and the interplay between Section 41 credit qualification and the treatment of research or experimental expenditures under Sections 174 and 174A.
The Federal Statutory Architecture of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and the Four-Part Test

Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) authorizes a general business credit against federal income tax liability for increasing qualified research activities. Eligibility for the credit is governed by 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), which requires every research activity to satisfy four cumulative statutory tests. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(1), those tests are applied separately to each business component of the taxpayer, so that a single project may contain both qualifying and non-qualifying components.
The Section 174 Eligibility Requirement

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), as amended by Public Law 119-21, research qualifies only if the expenditures with respect to such research are treated as domestic research or experimental (R&E) expenditures under IRC Section 174A. Before that amendment, the subparagraph referred to specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174. In either version, the threshold inquiry is the same: Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) provides that research or experimental expenditures are costs incident to the development or improvement of a product that represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, meaning activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. The expenditures must also be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business. The statutory and regulatory framework explicitly excludes the acquisition or improvement of land and the acquisition or improvement of depreciable or depletable property (IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b), although depreciation allowances on property used in research are themselves treated as research expenditures), expenditures for exploration for minerals, oil, or gas (IRC § 174(d)), and, under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6), ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, advertising and promotions, the acquisition of another person's patent, model, production, or process, and research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects.
The Technological Information Requirement

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is "technological in nature." As implemented in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3) and § 1.41-4(a)(4), this mandate has two interrelated parts: the research must be directed at eliminating uncertainty, and the process used to eliminate it must rest on the hard sciences. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3) provides that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4) provides that information is technological in nature only if the process of experimentation used to discover it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Research grounded in the social sciences, arts, humanities, economics, or business management therefore does not qualify, and 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(G) separately excludes research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities.
The Business Component and Permitted Purpose Requirement

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the taxpayer must intend that the application of the discovered technological information be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Section 41(d)(2)(B) defines a "business component" as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. This requirement works together with the qualified purpose rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(A), which provide that research is treated as conducted for a qualified purpose only if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality. Conversely, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) provides that research is not treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. The regulatory counterpart is Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), which states that a process of experimentation is undertaken for a qualified purpose if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component, and that research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors does not qualify. Both regulatory paragraphs are therefore cited in the table below for their respective functions.
The Process of Experimentation Requirement

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), "substantially all" of the activities of the research must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in Section 41(d)(3). Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) gives "substantially all" a fixed numerical meaning: the requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities for the business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (without regard to the shrinking-back rule), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. The regulation also specifies that the remaining 20 percent or less of activities need not be elements of a process of experimentation, provided they do not fall within the statutory exclusions of Section 41(d)(4).

body.text: Legislative History and Congressional Intent: The Tax Reform Act of 1986

The structure of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) originated in the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA '86), Public Law 99-514. Congress first enacted the federal research credit in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 as an incremental credit for research spending above a base amount. The 1981 version relied largely on the Section 174 concept of research and experimental expenditures and did not contain the separate definitional tests that now appear in Section 41(d). In the reports accompanying TRA '86 (including H.R. Rep. No. 99-426 and S. Rep. No. 99-313), Congress stated its concern that taxpayers had claimed the credit for activities that were not the type of high-technology research the incentive was meant to reward, including routine product development and expenditures unrelated to technological innovation.

To narrow the credit, TRA '86 added the statutory requirements that qualified research must be undertaken to discover information that is "technological in nature" and that substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a "process of experimentation" for a qualified purpose. In the General Explanation of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (commonly called the "Blue Book"), the staff of the Joint Committee on Taxation explained that research is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover the information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. That explanation was later carried into Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4).

The legislative history describes a process of experimentation as a process involving the evaluation of more than one alternative designed to achieve a result where the means of achieving that result is uncertain at the outset, and it allows for a process in which the taxpayer develops one or more hypotheses, designs and conducts experiments to test them, and refines or discards the hypotheses as part of a design process. The final regulations issued in 2004 (T.D. 9104) codified this approach in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), which provides that a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain at the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. The regulation lists modeling, simulation, and a systematic trial and error methodology as examples of evaluative methods.

CRS reports that the credit, enacted in 1981, was extended 16 times before the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 made it permanent, and its aggregate table shows that corporate taxpayers reported approximately $158 billion in qualified research expenses and claimed approximately $8.3 billion in research credits for 2007. The scale of those claims explains why the definitional limits of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) receive close attention on examination. For earlier year-by-year aggregate data, CRS directs readers to the IRS Statistics of Income corporation research credit tables.
Discovering Technological Information and Eliminating Objective Uncertainty

The requirement under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) that research be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature links the scientific domain of the inquiry to the presence of technical uncertainty. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4), a taxpayer satisfies the technological nature standard only if the underlying process of experimentation fundamentally relies on the principles of the physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and § 1.41-4(a)(4) also limit the scope of "discovery." Under § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), the discovery test does not require the taxpayer to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering, and a taxpayer is not required to succeed in developing a new or improved business component. This language replaced the "discovery test" of the 2001 final regulations (T.D. 8930), which had required information beyond the common knowledge of skilled professionals and which was withdrawn before taking effect. Under § 1.41-4(a)(4), a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and may rely on existing principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to satisfy the requirement, provided that applying those principles to the taxpayer's specific business component involves resolving uncertainty through a process of experimentation.

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component. Regulatory uncertainty therefore has three distinct technical dimensions. First, capability uncertainty arises when the taxpayer does not know whether the desired technical result or business component can be achieved at all. Second, method uncertainty arises when the taxpayer does not know the scientific or engineering process required to achieve that result. Third, appropriate design uncertainty exists when the specific technical architecture or design configuration of the final business component remains uncertain at the outset, even if the taxpayer already knows that the component is technically feasible and understands the general method required to construct it. Conversely, where the information available to the taxpayer at the outset already establishes the capability, the method, and the appropriate design, for example because the solution is readily available in published standards, vendor documentation, or the taxpayer's own prior work, there is no uncertainty of the kind the regulation requires, and the activity does not satisfy 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B) or § 41(d)(1)(C). The regulation measures uncertainty against the information available to the taxpayer rather than against the common knowledge of the industry, which is why the same activity can qualify for one taxpayer and fail for another with more relevant prior knowledge.
The Process of Experimentation, the 80 Percent Threshold, and the Shrinking-Back Rule

The process of experimentation test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5) is the most frequently litigated element of the four-part test before both the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and state tax authorities. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities.

To satisfy Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), the taxpayer's research activities must reflect three elements. The taxpayer must identify the uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the business component. Next, the taxpayer must identify one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty. Finally, the taxpayer must identify and conduct a process of evaluating those alternatives, for example through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology. The regulation adds that a process of experimentation is more than the evaluation of alternatives: it must be capable of evaluating more than one alternative, and the taxpayer must be able to show that it actually conducted the evaluation. Simply encountering a production defect, guessing at a fix, implementing an unmeasured adjustment, and resuming operations does not meet this standard. The taxpayer must test potential solutions against defined criteria until the uncertainty is resolved or the project is abandoned. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) also confirms that the taxpayer need not succeed: a process of experimentation that fails to produce a viable design can still qualify.
The "Substantially All" (80 Percent) Threshold

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), it is not enough that a project includes some experimental activity; substantially all of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) defines "substantially all" as 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities for that business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis. Expressed as a formula for a given business component, the requirement is: (research activities for the business component that constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose) divided by (total research activities for the business component) must be greater than or equal to 0.80, with both the numerator and the denominator measured on the same cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis.

If less than 80 percent of the research activities for a defined business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, the business component fails 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) at that level, and none of its associated expenditures are qualified research expenses at that level. If the fraction is 80 percent or more, all of the qualified research activities for that business component, including the non-experimental 20 percent or less, are eligible, subject to the statutory exclusions. The taxpayer must then apply the shrinking-back rule described below before concluding that no part of the project qualifies.
The Regulatory "Shrinking-Back" Rule

To prevent the complete disqualification of complex projects that combine routine implementation with genuine experimentation, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) establishes the "shrinking-back" rule. The requirements of Section 41(d) are first applied at the level of the discrete business component, meaning the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. If those requirements are not met at that level, they are applied at the level of the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention. This shrinking back continues until either a subset of elements satisfies the requirements or the most basic element is reached and fails. The regulation also states that the shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility; it is a rule that preserves credit for qualifying subsets, not a tool for the IRS to carve qualifying activities out of a component that already satisfies the tests.

For example, if an enterprise software deployment includes extensive routine data migration (non-qualifying) alongside the engineering of a novel predictive algorithm (qualifying), the deployment as a whole may fail the 80 percent test. By shrinking back the business component definition to the predictive algorithm sub-module, the taxpayer isolates the experimental core, tests that subset against the 80 percent threshold, and, if the subset satisfies all four tests, preserves the qualified research expenses directly attributable to it. Because the software in this example may be developed for the taxpayer's internal use, the taxpayer would also need to consider the additional internal use software requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(6), which apply on top of the four-part test of Section 41(d)(1).
Federal Judicial Interpretations of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)

Federal courts have consistently enforced the statutory boundaries of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), drawing distinctions between experimentation on the one hand and routine commercial engineering, quality control, production, or aesthetic design on the other, and placing the burden of substantiation on the taxpayer.
Union Carbide Corp. and Subsidiaries v. Commissioner: Process Research, Validation Testing, and Production Supplies

The Union Carbide research credit decision is Union Carbide Corp. and Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, 97 T.C.M. (CCH) 1207 (filed March 10, 2009), aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), cert. denied (2013). (Norwest Corp. and Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, the internal use software research credit case, is reported at 110 T.C. 454 (1998).)

In Union Carbide, the taxpayer claimed additional research credits for process improvement projects conducted at its chemical production plants in Hahnville, Louisiana during 1994 and 1995. The Tax Court applied the four tests of Section 41(d)(1) to the projects and held that some of them were qualified research while at least one project failed the process of experimentation requirement because it involved little more than validation testing of a solution whose design was not in doubt; the court made clear that confirming that a known solution works is not the same as evaluating alternatives to resolve uncertainty. The court also rejected the taxpayer's position that the cost of raw materials consumed in ordinary production runs, on which process research happened to be conducted, were supply QREs, holding that supplies the taxpayer would have used in production regardless of the research were not "used in the conduct of qualified research" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). The Second Circuit affirmed on the supply issue. For purposes of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), the case is regularly cited for the statement of the four-part test (the Seventh Circuit relied on it for that purpose in Little Sandy Coal) and for the principle that a process of experimentation requires an actual evaluation of alternatives rather than confirmation of a predetermined result. The broader framing of "systematic trial and error" versus "simple trial and error," and the rule that a taxpayer evaluating a single alternative must still conduct a documented series of experiments, is articulated most directly in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and in the California Office of Tax Appeals opinion in Appeal of Swat-Fame, Inc., discussed below.
Leon Max v. Commissioner: Excluding Style, Taste, and Routine Garment Testing

In Leon Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37 (filed March 29, 2021), the Tax Court examined research credits passed through to the shareholder of Leon Max, Inc., a women's apparel company, for 2011 and 2012. The claims arose from a credit study that concluded that the development of 32 of 35 sampled garments qualified. The taxpayer contended that its process of designing garments, fit testing, and fabric testing constituted research and experimentation under Section 41. The Tax Court rejected the claim on several grounds under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1). First, it held that the fabric testing was quality control testing excluded from research or experimental expenditures under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6), so the Section 174 test was not met. Second, relying on the Merriam-Webster definition of engineering ("the application of science and mathematics by which the properties of matter and the sources of energy in nature are made useful to people" or "the design and manufacture of complex products"), it held that fit testing and pattern work relied on knowledge common to designers and patternmakers rather than on principles of engineering or the hard sciences, so the technological information test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) was not met. Third, it held that the taxpayer did not show a process of experimentation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), and it observed that many of the design activities related to style, taste, and seasonal design factors, which cannot be a qualified purpose under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B). The court's analysis is consistent with its earlier decision in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, which also denied credits where the taxpayer could not show that its activities involved a process of experimentation. In 2023, the IRS cited Leon Max in Technical Advice Memorandum 202327015, which concluded that the presence of some non-permitted-purpose activities did not by itself prevent a retail apparel company from meeting the process of experimentation test, while reiterating that the taxpayer must substantiate that substantially all of its activities for the business component were elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.
Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner: Strict Enforcement of the 80 Percent Rule

In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's decision (T.C. Memo. 2021-15) disallowing research credits claimed for the 2014 tax year by the parent of Corn Island Shipyard, Inc., which designed and built 11 first-in-class vessels. The case turned on the "substantially all" requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6). The taxpayer argued that each vessel was a "pilot model" and that its production wages for building the vessels were qualified research expenses. The Seventh Circuit held that the taxpayer could not prevail under either view of the facts. If the vessels were not pilot models, the production activities would have to be included in the "substantially all" fraction, and the taxpayer had not shown what portion of those activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation. If the vessels were pilot models, the taxpayer still failed because it did not show how the models were used in a process of experimentation. For both alternatives, the court found that the taxpayer had failed to provide a principled way to determine the portion of employee activities that constituted elements of a process of experimentation. The decision confirms that the taxpayer bears the burden of documenting the numerator and the denominator of the 80 percent fraction, and that the inclusion of routine fabrication and supervision without such evidence leads to disallowance of the entire business component. The Tax Court also sustained an accuracy-related penalty.

body.text: State-Level Adoption and Modification of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1): California R&TC Section 23609

While 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) establishes the national definition of qualified research, state tax codes incorporate that definition with structural modifications. California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) Section 23609 adopts IRC § 41, including the four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), by reference, subject to state-specific rules. Taxpayers claiming the California credit must therefore demonstrate Section 174 eligibility, reliance on the hard sciences to discover technological information, a permitted functional purpose for a business component, and a process of experimentation that meets the 80 percent requirement, while also satisfying the California modifications described below. Senate Bill 711 (Stats. 2025, ch. 231), signed October 1, 2025, updated California's general IRC conformity date from January 1, 2015 to January 1, 2025 and amended Section 23609 for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025.
Geographic Nexus Requirements under R&TC § 23609(c)(2)

Under R&TC § 23609(c)(2), "qualified research" and "basic research" for California franchise and income tax purposes include only research conducted in California. This geographic restriction governs every category of qualified research expenses (QREs). For in-house wages to be eligible, they must be paid for qualified services performed in California; if an employee divides time between a laboratory in San Francisco and a testing facility in Nevada, the qualified wages must be allocated using reliable records, preferably contemporaneous time-tracking data. Third-party contract research expenses, which California takes into account under the 65 percent inclusion rule of IRC § 41(b)(3)(A), qualify only to the extent the contractor performs the research in California, and the taxpayer bears the burden of establishing where the work was done. The federal statute treats amounts paid to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research as in-house research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). Because California limits the credit to research conducted in California, taxpayers that claim computer rental or cloud hosting charges should be prepared to show that the research, and the computing resources used to perform it, are attributable to California.
Modified Gross Receipts and Anti-Double-Dipping Rules

California modifies the base amount calculation for the regular credit by redefining "gross receipts." Under R&TC § 23609(i), gross receipts for purposes of the California credit include only gross receipts from the sale of property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of the taxpayer's trade or business that is delivered or shipped to a purchaser within California. Whereas the federal computation uses the taxpayer's total gross receipts, California's definition excludes receipts from services, rents, royalties, and out-of-state shipments, which can change the fixed-base percentage and base amount substantially relative to the federal return. The 2023 OTA proceeding in Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corp. illustrates the practical effect for a service provider whose California gross receipts were small under this definition.

Under R&TC § 23609(c)(1), California also prevents a double benefit for the same expenditure: any amount paid or incurred for tangible personal property that is eligible for the exemption from sales or use tax under R&TC Section 6378 is excluded from California QREs. Section 6378 provides a partial sales and use tax exemption for certain property used in manufacturing and research and development. Taxpayers must therefore coordinate the purchase-level exemption with the income tax credit computation for qualifying supplies.
The 2025 California Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Reform and Carryforward Rules

Historically, California offered two computation methods: the regular research credit, equal to 15 percent of current-year California QREs exceeding the base amount (plus 24 percent of basic research payments), and the Alternative Incremental Research Credit (AIRC, often called the AIC). SB 711 repealed the AIRC for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025 and adopted the federal Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) of IRC § 41(c)(4) with reduced state rates. Under R&TC § 23609(h)(2)(A), clause (i) substitutes 3 percent for the federal 14 percent rate, so the California ASC equals 3 percent of current-year California QREs that exceed 50 percent of the taxpayer's average California QREs for the three preceding taxable years. Clause (ii) substitutes 1.3 percent for the federal 6 percent rate that applies when the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years, so in that case the California ASC equals 1.3 percent of current-year California QREs.

Taxpayers that previously used the repealed AIRC must make a new election on California Form FTB 3523 for the 2025 taxable year, choosing either the regular credit or the ASC, because prior AIRC elections do not carry over to the new method. The FTB has issued guidance to that effect, and practitioners have noted that the ASC election should be modeled carefully because of its election rules. Despite the lower ASC rates, California retains a structural advantage over federal law: unused federal research credits may be carried back one year and forward 20 years under IRC § 39, while under R&TC § 23609(f) excess California research credits may be carried over to succeeding years until the credit has been exhausted, with no expiration date.
California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) Jurisprudence

The Franchise Tax Board (FTB) and the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA), the independent appeals body established by the Taxpayer Transparency and Fairness Act of 2017, apply the process of experimentation requirement of R&TC § 23609 and 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) strictly. In its precedential opinion Appeal of Swat-Fame, Inc. et al., 2020-OTA-046P, the OTA denied in full refund claims of approximately $2.4 million in California research credits for the 2008 through 2012 tax years filed by a designer of women's and girls' apparel. The opinion establishes three principles for California audits. First, the OTA read the process of experimentation requirement in the scientific-method sense, holding that taking business steps to resolve a commercial uncertainty is not enough and that a trial-and-error approach qualifies only if it is systematic. Second, where a taxpayer relies on systematic trial and error, including the evaluation of a single alternative, it must document a series of experiments; Swat-Fame did not, and for one sample project involving shrinkage of denim Bermuda shorts the OTA found that although some fabric treatments may have involved trial and error, the record did not show a systematic process, such as logs of methods tested in wash trials. Third, the OTA applied the IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) exclusion for style, taste, cosmetic, and seasonal design factors, finding that a significant portion of the project work served aesthetic purposes, and concluded that the taxpayer failed to prove that 80 percent or more of its activities for any sampled project constituted elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. The OTA and later opinions also cite Swat-Fame for the propositions that credits are a matter of legislative grace and that the taxpayer bears the burden of proving entitlement.

Later OTA opinions apply the same evidentiary standard across technology sectors. In Appeal of First Solar, Inc., 2023-OTA-532P (precedential, September 19, 2023; OTA Case No. 21088511), the OTA sustained the FTB's denial of research credit carryforwards used in 2013 that had been generated in 2006 through 2009 by a solar module manufacturer. The OTA held that audited financial statements reporting a total research and development line item could inform an estimate of amounts but could not establish that activities were qualified research; that an IRS directive accepting audited research figures for administrative purposes does not decide qualification under IRC § 41(d); that patents, which can support the technological-in-nature and business component tests under the regulatory safe harbor, do not establish the Section 174 test or the process of experimentation test; and that credible but general testimony from a former technical executive did not show that substantially all of the research was a qualified process of experimentation or separate California activities from activities elsewhere. In Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corp. & Subsidiaries, 2023-OTA-540 (nonprecedential, September 20, 2023), the OTA addressed its jurisdiction over certain refund claims, enterprise zone credit issues, and the California regular research credit, and held that the taxpayer failed to substantiate its claimed credit because it relied primarily on employee surveys prepared after the research activities had concluded.
Comparative State Tax Frameworks: New York and Massachusetts

Other states with significant research activity tie their incentives to the IRC § 41 definition of qualified research, including 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), while differing in rates, caps, eligibility, and administration.
New York Department of Taxation and Finance Guidance

New York's principal research credit for program participants is the Excelsior Research and Development Tax Credit under the Excelsior Jobs Program (N.Y. Economic Development Law § 355(3); 5 NYCRR § 193.1), administered by Empire State Development with the credit claimed through the Department of Taxation and Finance. Because the credit is computed from the participant's federal research credit, it incorporates the federal definition of qualified research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1). The statute provides a credit equal to 50 percent of the portion of the participant's federal research and development tax credit that relates to research and development expenditures in New York State, limited to 6 percent of the research and development expenditures attributable to activities conducted in New York State (7 percent for a qualified semiconductor supply chain project and 8 percent for a qualified green project or green CHIPS project). Excelsior credits are refundable. Participation is limited to businesses in strategic industries that meet job and investment commitments. New York also offers a separate refundable Life Sciences Research and Development Tax Credit under Tax Law § 43.
Massachusetts Department of Revenue Guidance

Under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 63, Section 38M (M.G.L. c. 63, § 38M), the traditional Massachusetts research credit under subsection (a) equals 10 percent of qualified research expenses above the base amount plus 15 percent of basic research payments, with terms defined by reference to IRC § 41 as amended and in effect on August 12, 1991. Subsection (b) provides an alternative simplified method (ASM), which uses the Code as in effect on January 1, 2014 and, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2021, equals 10 percent of qualified research expenses exceeding 50 percent of the average qualified research expenses for the three preceding taxable years. Both methods are limited to research conducted in the Commonwealth, and the credit is claimed on Schedule RC, administered by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue (DOR). The DOR applies the federal technological-in-nature requirement because the credit is defined by reference to IRC § 41, so research must rely on the hard sciences and studies in economics or business management do not qualify. Under § 38M(g), unused credits may be carried forward for 15 taxable years, and credits disallowed by the limitation in § 38M(e) (which generally limits the credit to 100 percent of the first $25,000 of excise plus 75 percent of the remaining excise) may be carried to any subsequent taxable year without expiration. Finally, in TIR 25-3 (May 9, 2025), the DOR acknowledged the Appellate Tax Board's 2024 decision in State Street Corporation v. Commissioner of Revenue (ATB 2024-201) and confirmed that financial institutions subject to the excise under M.G.L. c. 63, § 2 may claim the § 38M credit, including by amended return or abatement application for open years, and that the DOR will not enforce a proposed regulatory limit that would otherwise have restricted use of the ASM on such amended claims. The process of experimentation requirement continues to apply to these claims.

body.text: The Statutory Intersection of Section 41(d)(1)(A) and Sections 174 and 174A

Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) conditions credit eligibility on whether expenditures are treated as research or experimental expenditures, legislative changes to Section 174 directly affect Section 41 compliance and corporate tax accounting. Before 2022, IRC § 174 permitted taxpayers to deduct research or experimental expenditures currently or to elect amortization over at least 60 months. Under amendments enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, IRC § 174 required taxpayers to capitalize specified research or experimental expenditures, expressly including software development costs under IRC § 174(c)(3), and to amortize them ratably over 5 years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research, beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year. The IRS implemented the change as an automatic accounting method change under IRC § 481 through Revenue Procedure 2023-11.

Public Law 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025, added IRC Section 174A. For amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, Section 174A allows a current deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures (with an election to capitalize and amortize over not less than 60 months), while foreign research or experimental expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization under Section 174. The same law amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to refer to domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A. Eligible small business taxpayers that meet the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test (about $31 million for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024) may elect to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and all taxpayers may elect to deduct remaining unamortized domestic expenditures from 2022 through 2024 either in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 or ratably over two years. The IRS provided procedures in Revenue Procedure 2025-28.
Scope Divergence Between Section 174 / 174A R&E and Section 41 QREs

While every Section 41 QRE must satisfy the Section 174 or 174A eligibility requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), Section 41 QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) are a narrower subset of total research or experimental expenditures. A taxpayer's Section 174 or 174A pool routinely exceeds its Section 41 QRE pool because Section 174 and 174A encompass costs that are excluded from the credit computation, such as patent procurement legal fees, overhead allocations, and depreciation allowances on research equipment, and because foreign research expenditures are R&E expenditures under Section 174 but are excluded from qualified research by IRC § 41(d)(4)(F). The interaction is also governed by IRC § 280C(c). For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, as amended by Public Law 119-21, § 280C(c)(1) requires taxpayers to reduce their domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A (whether deducted or capitalized) by the amount of the Section 41 credit, unless they make a timely election under § 280C(c)(2) on an original return to claim a reduced credit. Under that election the credit is reduced by the product of the credit and the maximum corporate tax rate, so a corporation claims 79 percent of the otherwise allowable credit. For taxable years beginning in 2022 through 2024, the TCJA version of § 280C(c)(1) reduced the capitalized amount only to the extent the credit exceeded the amount allowable as a deduction, which in practice rarely required a reduction.

body.text: Post-OBBBA Federal IRC § 174A Expensing and California's Treatment

Public Law 119-21 enacted IRC Section 174A, restoring current expensing for domestic research or experimental expenditures for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while preserving 15-year amortization for foreign research or experimental expenditures.

California operates under a selective, fixed-date conformity regime. SB 711 updated the state's general IRC conformity date to January 1, 2025, a date that precedes the July 4, 2025 enactment of Public Law 119-21, so OBBBA's changes are not part of California law. California never adopted the TCJA amendments to Section 174, and SB 711 continued that nonconformity: California does not adopt the federal capitalization and amortization rules for research and experimental expenditures under either Section 174 or Section 174A, and both domestic and foreign research expenditures remain deductible for California purposes under the pre-TCJA rules. In practice, a corporation therefore deducts its domestic research expenditures currently on both its federal return (under Section 174A) and its California return (under California's pre-TCJA Section 174 conformity), while foreign research expenditures are amortized over 15 years federally but deducted for California purposes. Taxpayers that capitalized research expenditures federally in 2022 through 2024 should already have reported a federal-state difference for California for those years. Other states analyze Section 41 claims with reference to the same federal definitions; for example, states that adopt IRC § 41(b) apply the federal rule that property subject to depreciation is not a supply QRE.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Applying 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and R&TC § 23609 to Software and Hardware Integration

To demonstrate the quantitative and legal operation of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6), the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2), the Swat-Fame documentation standard, and California R&TC § 23609, consider the following hypothetical scenario. All figures are illustrative.
Hypothetical Fact Pattern: AeroTech Systems (Tax Year 2025)

AeroTech Systems, a hypothetical calendar-year C corporation headquartered in San Jose, California, incurs $1,000,000 of engineering and development expenditures during the 2025 tax year to build an autonomous drone navigation module that it will sell to customers. The overall project has two technical phases. In Phase 1 (conceptualization and routine engineering), AeroTech purchases commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) drone motors and assigns software engineers to write standard application programming interface (API) integrations linking those motors to an existing open-source flight controller. In Phase 2 (resolving technical uncertainty through experimentation), AeroTech attempts to develop a new edge-computing LiDAR data-processing algorithm that will enable autonomous navigation through dense forest environments. At the outset of Phase 2, AeroTech does not know whether the result can be achieved or what the appropriate design of the algorithm should be, because existing LiDAR processing models require so much processing power that they drain the drone battery almost immediately. To resolve this uncertainty, the engineering team formulates a hypothesis (that a customized edge-computing data-culling algorithm can reduce LiDAR data load by 40 percent without reducing obstacle detection speed) and executes a systematic testing protocol, running iterative computational simulations against baseline models, modifying code parameters in 5 percent increments, and logging CPU usage and crash rates in a simulated forest environment.
Step 1: Applying the Four-Part Test, the 80 Percent Rule, and the Shrinking-Back Rule

Evaluating both phases against 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) shows how the statutory filter operates in practice. Phase 1 fails the technological information test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and the process of experimentation test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). Writing standard API connectors to link COTS hardware relies on publicly available documentation and routine programming techniques; the information available to AeroTech at the outset already establishes the capability, the method, and the appropriate design, and no alternatives are evaluated.

Phase 2, by contrast, satisfies all four tests. The expenditures are experimental software development costs that are domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A)); the inquiry relies fundamentally on computer science to eliminate uncertainty about capability and appropriate design (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)); the algorithm is intended to improve the function, performance, and reliability of the navigation module, a business component held for sale (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), § 41(d)(3)(A), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)); and the iterative simulation protocol, which evaluates parameter alternatives against logged CPU and crash data, is a systematic evaluation of alternatives that meets Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and the documentation standard applied by the OTA in Swat-Fame (§ 41(d)(1)(C)).

The 80 percent requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) is tested first at the level of the business component, the navigation module as a whole. Suppose AeroTech's time records show that, measured by cost, 60 percent of the module's research activities were Phase 2 experimental activities and 40 percent were Phase 1 routine integration. At the module level, 0.60 is less than 0.80, so the module fails the substantially all requirement. Under the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2), AeroTech then applies the four tests to the most significant subset of elements, the LiDAR data-processing algorithm sub-module. Suppose the records for that sub-module show that 90 percent of its research activities, measured by cost, were elements of the simulation-based process of experimentation. Because 0.90 is at least 0.80, the sub-module satisfies 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), and the QREs directly attributable to Phase 2 are preserved. The Phase 1 costs are excluded from QREs, although they may still be research or experimental expenditures for Section 174A purposes if they are costs incident to the development of the product.
Step 2: Recomputing the Hypothetical Expense Allocation and Tax Credit Calculations

For the computation below, assume that the $1,000,000 expenditure pool shown in the table consists of costs attributable to the qualifying Phase 2 sub-module after applying the shrinking-back rule, so that the 80 percent requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) is satisfied for every line item. The federal and California QRE determinations then proceed line by line as shown. Federal eligible QREs equal $500,000 + $200,000 + $65,000 + $100,000 + $0 = $865,000. California eligible QREs under R&TC § 23609(c)(2) equal $500,000 + $0 + $65,000 + $0 + $0 = $565,000.

body.text: Applying the ASC rates for the 2025 tax year under IRC § 41(c)(4) and R&TC § 23609(h)(2)(A) (elected for California on Form FTB 3523) shows the arithmetic effect of these rules. In the first scenario, assume AeroTech's average annual federal QREs for 2022 through 2024 were $600,000 and its average annual California QREs for the same period were $400,000. The federal ASC base equals 50 percent of $600,000, or $300,000, yielding federal excess QREs of $865,000 − $300,000 = $565,000 and a 14 percent federal ASC of $565,000 × 0.14 = $79,100. If AeroTech makes the reduced credit election under IRC § 280C(c)(2), the federal credit becomes $79,100 × 0.79 = $62,489, and AeroTech is not required to reduce its Section 174A deduction by the credit; without the election, the full $79,100 credit is claimed and the Section 174A expenditures are reduced by $79,100. On the California return in the same scenario, the California ASC base equals 50 percent of $400,000, or $200,000, yielding California excess QREs of $565,000 − $200,000 = $365,000 and a 3 percent California ASC of $365,000 × 0.03 = $10,950.

In the second scenario, assume AeroTech had no QREs in at least one of the three preceding taxable years. Federally, IRC § 41(c)(4)(B) sets the ASC at 6 percent of current-year QREs, or $865,000 × 0.06 = $51,900. For California, R&TC § 23609(h)(2)(A)(ii) sets the ASC at 1.3 percent of current-year California QREs, or $565,000 × 0.013 = $7,345. For the treatment of the underlying spending, AeroTech may deduct its domestic research or experimental expenditures on its 2025 federal return under IRC § 174A. Of the $1,000,000 total, the $100,000 cost of the depreciable server is not a research or experimental expenditure and is recovered through depreciation, with the depreciation allowance for the year treated as a Section 174A expenditure; the remaining $900,000 (including the $200,000 of Texas wages and the full $100,000 contract research payment, since the 65 percent limit applies only to the credit computation) consists of domestic research or experimental expenditures. On its California return, AeroTech also deducts those expenditures currently, because California does not adopt the federal capitalization rules of Section 174 or Section 174A.

body.text: Technical Substantiation and Audit Defense Implications

Under the standards applied in Union Carbide, Leon Max, Little Sandy Coal, Swat-Fame, First Solar, and Electronic Data Systems, after-the-fact oral assertions, surveys prepared after the research ended, audited financial statement line items, and generalized cost-center allocations are not enough on their own to prove that activities satisfy 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1).

Instead, substantiating that an activity satisfies 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) calls for technical records created during the research, such as statements of the technical uncertainty, the hypotheses or design alternatives considered, simulation and trial logs, failure analyses, code-versioning histories, and engineering diagrams. Those records should be paired with time-tracking detailed enough to compute the 80 percent "substantially all" fraction under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) for each business component (or for a properly defined subset under the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2)), to tie the qualifying activities to the claimed wage, supply, computer-use, and contract research amounts, and to establish in-state performance under state statutes such as California R&TC § 23609(c)(2). The federal Form 6765 requirements that the IRS has phased in for business-component-level information make the same point from the reporting side: the credit is claimed and defended one business component at a time.
